title: the Nayanars
hook: a hunter who worships Shiva all wrong, and all right

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars once more. Nammalvar, silent under the tamarind, answered a riddle in two short lines, and then began to sing.
screen: `THE ALVARS.` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.`

segments.voice: Every morning a priest climbs a hill to a small shrine of Shiva, and every morning he finds a mess. Bits of meat on the stone. Flowers that look like they've been stuck in somebody's hair. Water splashed everywhere, as if someone spat it. He cleans it all, does the worship properly, and goes home upset. Next morning, the same. Someone is worshiping here, and doing it all wrong.
screen: `A MESS AT SHIVA'S SHRINE.` → `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME.` → `WHO IS DOING THIS?`

segments.voice: Today the path crosses to the Nayanars, the Tamil saints of Shiva. Tradition counts sixty-three, and their lives are told in a long Tamil work, the Periya Puranam. They're a mixed crowd: kings and housewives, a potter, a washerman, a hunter. Today's is the hunter, Tinnan. Tracking in the hills, he comes across the shrine, and something in him breaks open. He has no idea how worship is done, so he does what a hunter would do for someone he loves. He carries water in his mouth, because he has no pot. He brings flowers in his hair, because his hands hold his bow. And he brings meat he has roasted and tasted first, so only the best goes to Shiva. That's the mess. In the story, Shiva tells the priest in a dream to hide and watch. So the priest is crouched behind the shrine the day the image's eye starts to bleed. Tinnan tries herbs. Nothing. So he takes an arrow, digs out his own eye, and presses it into place. The bleeding stops. Then the image's other eye starts to bleed. Tinnan sets his foot on the spot, so he can find it once he's blind, and lifts the arrow to his second eye. And Shiva's hand comes out of the stone and stops him. From then on, the story says, he's called Kannappa, a name tied to his eye. There's a thread here. Krishna's village loved him without a rulebook. Andal wore the garland first. Now a hunter tastes the meat first. Again and again, love breaks the rule of the untouched offering, and the priest who knows every rule is the one sent to watch.
screen: `THE NAYANARS: SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `WATER IN HIS MOUTH, MEAT TASTED FIRST.` · `HIS OWN EYE FOR THE BLEEDING ONE.` · `SHIVA'S HAND STOPS HIM.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and think of the clumsiest way you've ever shown love: a burnt meal, a gift that missed, words that came out wrong. Look at it the way the story looks at Tinnan, seeing what you were actually trying to give, and let it be enough. If you pray, offer whatever you have today, clumsy as it is, to God by any name you use.
The Nayanars. The Tamil saints of Shiva, whose lives the Periya Puranam tells. Kannappa is the hunter who offered his own eye.
Your line: Kannappa's eye. A hunter with no rulebook, remembered as a saint. Day nine hundred ten, done.

howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus in Tamil Nadu honor the Nayanars in temples, often with images of them in a row, and Kannappa is especially remembered at the Shiva temple of Srikalahasti.

chat.says: Why is a hunter who did the worship all wrong honored as a saint of Shiva?
options: He gave the best he had out of love, and in the story Shiva himself stopped him.
He later learned the proper rites from the priest and did them perfectly.
He was really a priest in disguise, testing the temple's rules.
chat.meaning: Tinnan didn't know the rules; he gave water, flowers and meat out of love, then his own eye. Shiva's hand stopped him.
